allowed_dependency_manifest.content: Let n, k, l ∈ Z with 0 ≤ k, l ≤ n. Define R(q) = [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q in the natural rational-function setting for Gaussian q-binomial coefficients. If R(q) lies in a polynomial ring in q (i.e., R(q) has only finitely many nonnegative powers of q with coefficients in the relevant coefficient ring), then when written as R(q) = Σ_i c_i q^i, every coefficient c_i satisfies c_i ≥ 0.

forbidden_claims.statement_nl: Let [n choose k]_q denote the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient. Prove that for all integers n, k, l with 0 ≤ k, l ≤ n, if [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q is a polynomial in q, then that polynomial has only nonnegative coefficients.

payload.role_in_assembly: Provides the finite-dimensionality hypothesis needed to apply the Hilbert-series positivity lemma to the graded quotient ring produced by L4.

domain_restrictions: R(q) must be well-defined as a formal expression: [n choose l]_q ≠ 0 and division is interpreted in the ambient field/ring where Gaussian coefficients live (typically Q(q) or a localization of Z[q])
the premise “is a polynomial in q” means R(q) has no negative powers of q (i.e., R(q) ∈ coefficient_ring[q] for some coefficient ring)

payload.statement_nl: Let d be a nonnegative integer and let w_1, ..., w_d be positive integers. Give S := Q[x_1, ..., x_d] the grading deg(x_i) = w_i; when d = 0 interpret S as Q. Then for every integer m >= 0 the homogeneous component S_m is finite-dimensional over Q. Consequently, if I is a homogeneous ideal of S, then for every integer m >= 0 the homogeneous component (S/I)_m is finite-dimensional over Q.

result_payload.proof_nl:
We prove the two assertions in order.

First, consider the weighted grading on S.

If d = 0, then by the convention in the statement we have S = Q. In this case the only nonzero homogeneous piece is degree 0: namely S_0 = Q and S_m = 0 for every m > 0. Hence each S_m is finite-dimensional over Q.

Now assume d >= 1. For a = (a_1, ..., a_d) in Z_{>=0}^d, write x^a := x_1^{a_1} ... x_d^{a_d}. Since deg(x_i) = w_i, the monomial x^a is homogeneous of weighted degree

a_1 w_1 + ... + a_d w_d.

Therefore, for any fixed m >= 0,

S_m = span_Q { x^a : a in Z_{>=0}^d and a_1 w_1 + ... + a_d w_d = m }.

Let

A_m := { a in Z_{>=0}^d : a_1 w_1 + ... + a_d w_d = m }.

We claim that A_m is finite. Indeed, if a belongs to A_m, then for each i we have

0 <= a_i w_i <= m.

Because w_i > 0, this implies

0 <= a_i <= m / w_i,

hence in particular

0 <= a_i <= floor(m / w_i).

So each coordinate a_i has only finitely many possibilities, namely 0, 1, ..., floor(m / w_i). Thus

A_m \subseteq \prod_{i=1}^d {0,1,...,floor(m / w_i)},

and therefore A_m is finite. Consequently S_m is spanned by finitely many monomials.

These monomials are linearly independent over Q (distinct monomials in a polynomial ring are linearly independent), so they form a Q-basis of S_m. Hence

dim_Q S_m = |A_m| < infinity.

This proves the first assertion: for every m >= 0, the homogeneous component S_m is finite-dimensional over Q.

Now let I be a homogeneous ideal of S. Because I is homogeneous, the quotient S/I inherits the grading, and the degree-m component is the image of S_m under the quotient map pi : S -> S/I. More precisely, the restriction

pi|_{S_m} : S_m -> (S/I)_m

is surjective, and its kernel is exactly I \cap S_m. Therefore, by the first isomorphism theorem,

(S/I)_m \cong S_m / (I \cap S_m).

But I \cap S_m is a Q-subspace of the finite-dimensional Q-vector space S_m. A quotient of a finite-dimensional vector space by a subspace is again finite-dimensional. Hence (S/I)_m is finite-dimensional over Q for every m >= 0.

So both claims follow.
result_payload.proof_summary: For fixed m, the degree-m monomials are indexed by nonnegative integer solutions of a_1 w_1 + ... + a_d w_d = m. Since each w_i > 0, every solution satisfies 0 <= a_i <= floor(m / w_i), so only finitely many such monomials exist. They form a basis of S_m, hence S_m is finite-dimensional. If I is homogeneous, then (S/I)_m is naturally isomorphic to S_m / (I \cap S_m), a quotient of a finite-dimensional vector space, so it is also finite-dimensional.

used_external_facts: Distinct monomials in a polynomial ring over Q are linearly independent.
A quotient of a finite-dimensional vector space by a subspace is finite-dimensional.
